lesson.title: The Middle 50 Percent: Measuring Spread with the IQR
lesson.summary: The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle half of a dataset and, unlike the range, resists distortion from outliers, making it a key tool for detecting unusual values.
lesson.body:
When you first learn to describe the spread of a distribution, the range (maximum minus minimum) seems like the obvious tool. But the range has a serious weakness: it depends entirely on the two most extreme values in the dataset. A single unusually high or low score, one that might be a typo, a measurement error, or a genuinely rare event, can inflate the range and give a misleading picture of how spread out the typical data really are. The interquartile range, or IQR, fixes this by ignoring the extremes entirely and focusing on where the middle half of the data actually lives.

The IQR is built directly from quartiles, the three values that split an ordered dataset into four equal-sized groups. The first quartile, Q1, is the median of the lower half of the data; the third quartile, Q3, is the median of the upper half. The interquartile range is simply IQR equals Q3 minus Q1. Because it is calculated from the middle 50 percent of the data, moving the smallest or largest observation around, even by a huge amount, usually does not change the IQR at all. Statisticians call this property resistance, and it is the same reason the median resists outliers while the mean does not.

Consider fourteen quiz scores from a class, one of which is unusually low because a student was absent for most of the period: 15, 62, 65, 68, 72, 75, 78, 80, 82, 85, 88, 92, 95, 98. With 14 values, the lower half consists of the first seven scores (15, 62, 65, 68, 72, 75, 78), whose median is the fourth value, 68; this is Q1. The upper half consists of the last seven scores (80, 82, 85, 88, 92, 95, 98), whose median is 88; this is Q3. So IQR equals 88 minus 68, which is 20 points. That single number tells you the middle half of the class scored within a 20 point band, regardless of how badly the absent student did.

The IQR also powers a standard rule for flagging outliers: any value below Q1 minus 1.5 times the IQR, or above Q3 plus 1.5 times the IQR, is considered a potential outlier. In the quiz example, 1.5 times the IQR is 1.5 times 20, which equals 30, so the lower fence sits at 68 minus 30, or 38, and the upper fence sits at 88 plus 30, or 118. The score of 15 falls well below 38, so the rule correctly flags it as an outlier worth investigating, while every other score stays safely inside the fences.

This 1.5 times IQR rule is exactly what draws the whiskers on a boxplot and decides which points get plotted individually as dots beyond them. Because the IQR describes spread without being fooled by a handful of extreme scores, it pairs naturally with the median as a resistant summary of center and spread, the pair you should reach for whenever a distribution is skewed or contains outliers. When you move on to assessing whether a distribution is approximately normal, you will see the IQR again: a normal distribution has a very predictable relationship between its standard deviation and its IQR, and a big departure from that relationship is one more clue that a dataset is not actually shaped like a bell curve.
